segments.narration: A five-story Antarctic waterfall bleeds bright crimson red. Discovered on Taylor Glacier in 1911, it looked like fresh blood pouring over pure white ice.
Scientists originally blamed red algae. But tests found zero plant life—and revealed the water stayed liquid far below freezing temperatures.
How could flowing water exist in a frozen wasteland? Researchers scanned four hundred meters down with deep radar and uncovered the hidden source.
Trapped below was an ancient, super-salty lake sealed without light for two million years. Its massive iron content rusts instantly when hitting air.
That red waterfall is actually liquid rust. Even wilder, ancient microbes thrive inside it without oxygen—proving life can survive on alien worlds.

verdicts.claim: In 1911, explorers discovered a red waterfall pouring out of Taylor Glacier in Antarctica.
verdicts.note: The reference states that the reddish deposit was discovered in 1911 by Thomas Griffith Taylor at Taylor Glacier, Antarctica.

verdicts.claim: Early theories attributed the red color of Blood Falls to red algae, but testing revealed no algae was present.
verdicts.note: The text confirms early pioneers attributed the red color to red algae, but it was later proven to be due to iron oxides.

verdicts.claim: Researchers used radio-echo sounding radar to scan hundreds of meters beneath Taylor Glacier.
verdicts.note: The provided text mentions using an IceMole probe to melt into the glacier, but does not mention radio-echo sounding radar.

verdicts.claim: Blood Falls gets its red color from iron-rich subglacial brine rusting upon exposure to atmospheric oxygen.
verdicts.note: The text confirms hydrous ferric oxides (rust) are deposited when ferrous ions in the unfrozen saltwater oxidize upon contact with atmospheric oxygen.

verdicts.claim: Microbes survive inside the oxygen-free subglacial reservoir feeding Blood Falls by metabolizing iron and sulfate.
verdicts.note: The reference notes that microbes survive in an oxygen-free ecosystem feeding on Blood Falls brine by metabolizing sulfate and ferric ions.
